title: Benin Palace Plaque
craftSpec: Pigments hand-ground in linseed or walnut oil over sized and primed support; layered from dark underpainting (imprimatura) to opaque highlights.
region: Nigeria (Royal Palace of the Oba, Benin City, Edo State)
note: Hundreds of rectangular plaques like this one hung on the pillars of the royal palace in Benin City, fixed by nails punched through them. They were cast by the lost-wax method, in brass that came partly from bracelet-shaped ingots bought from Portuguese traders. British forces took them when they sacked the city in 1897, and the Foreign Office gave a large number to the British Museum. From 1950 the museum sold more than 30 to the Nigerian government as duplicates; the sales stopped in 1972.

Mr. Jonathon Chambers left his house on Maple Street at exactly seven o'clock in the evening and set out on the daily walk he had taken, at the same time, come rain or snow, for twenty solid years.

Even the man at the Red Star confectionery, where he bought his cigar, remained silent while the purchase was being made. On which the Prince of Glory dy'd,
My richest gain I count but loss,

Save in the death of Christ my God;
All the vain things that charm me most,
I sacrifice them to his blood.

See from his head, his hands, his feet,
Sorrow and love flow mingled down;
Did e'er such love and sorrow meet?
Or thorns compose so rich a crown?

His dying crimson like a robe
Spreads o'er his body on the tree;
Then am I dead to all the globe,
And all the globe is dead to me.

Were the whole realm of nature mine,
That were a present far too small;
Love so amazing, so divine,
Demands my soul, my life, my all.

fullText: An adulteress was forgiven who passed by a dog at a well; for the dog was holding out his tongue from thirst, which was near killing him; and the woman took off her boot, and tied it to the end of her garment, and drew water for the dog, and gave him to drink; and she was forgiven for that act.
